Title: 'Neuer Beweis für die Umkehrung der Reihen' (A new proof of the reversion of series). It is dated Dec. 12. The bundle and the previous page, dated Nov. 12 and citing Comm. Gott. XVI, point to 1813.

§1. Gauss takes T = t + αt² + βt³ + γt⁴ + … and U = u + αu² + βu³ + … (the same power series in two variables). He expands −log(1 − T/U) in powers of t: −log(1−T/U) = U′t + U″t² + U‴t³ + … . The coefficients U^{(k)} are Laurent series in u whose lowest term is u^{−k}. (The image has a minus sign before 'log' here; the machine transcription drops it.)

§2. Because U − T = (u − t)·[1 + α(u+t) + β(u²+ut+t²) + γ(u³+u²t+ut²+t³) + …], he writes
1 − T/U = (1 − t/u)·[1 + α(u+t) + β(u²+ut+t²) + …]/[1 + αu + βu² + …].
Taking logarithms:
−log(1−T/U) = t/u + t²/(2u²) + t³/(3u³) + … − log(1 + [αt + β(ut+t²) + γ(u²t+ut²+t³) + …]/[1 + αu + βu² + …]).
The last logarithm is an ordinary power series in t and u, since the denominator is invertible at u = 0. Hence U^{(k)} − 1/(k u^k) contains no negative powers of u. Consequently, in −log(1−T/U) the coefficient of u^{−m} (m ≥ 1) is exactly t^m/m.

Second expansion. He writes −log(1−T/U) = Σ_n T^n U^{−n}/n and sets U^{−n} = u^{−n}(1 + (n,1)u + (n,2)u² + …). Thus (n,j) = [u^j](u/U)^n. This gives the double array
T u^{−1} + (1,1)T + (1,2)Tu + … + ½T²u^{−2} + ½(2,1)T²u^{−1} + ½(2,2)T² + … + ⅓T³u^{−3} + ⅓(3,1)T³u^{−2} + ⅓(3,2)T³u^{−1} + … .

Comparing coefficients of u^{−1} in the two expansions:
T + ½(2,1)T² + ⅓(3,2)T³ + ¼(4,3)T⁴ + … = t.
Comparing coefficients of u^{−2} (multiplied by 2):
T² + (2/3)(3,1)T³ + (2/4)(4,2)T⁴ + (2/5)(5,3)T⁵ + … = t².
In general, comparing coefficients of u^{−m} (multiplied by m):
T^m + (m/(m+1))(m+1,1)T^{m+1} + (m/(m+2))(m+2,2)T^{m+2} + … = t^m.
In modern form: [T^n] t^m = (m/n)[u^{n−m}](u/U(u))^n. This is the Lagrange–Bürmann inversion formula for the inverse series t(T). In effect it is a formal-residue proof using the two-variable logarithmic kernel log((U−T)/(u−t)).

Addendum, 'Das Resultat der Umkehrung'. Let X = x + a x^{1+λ} + b x^{1+2λ} + … and x = X + A X^{1+λ} + B X^{1+2λ} + … be mutually inverse. Then
([X^M] x^m)/m = ([x^{−m}] X^{−M})/M = ([x^{M−m}] (X/x)^{−M})/M.

'Einfachster Beweis' (simplest proof). He embeds the problem in Lagrange's equation x = t + X f(x), with f(x) = 1/(1 + a x^λ + b x^{2λ} + …) = x/X(x). The original problem is the case t = 0 (my reading). Lagrange's series reads
φ(x) = φ(t) + X φ′(t)f(t) + (X²/2) d[φ′(t)f(t)²]/dt + (X³/6) d²[φ′(t)f(t)³]/dt² + … .
He takes φ = f^m. A first attempt with f^{−m} is struck out. Then φ′f^n = (m/(m+n)) d(f^{m+n})/dt, so
f(x)^m = f(t)^m + (m/(m+1)) X d f(t)^{m+1}/dt + ½ (m/(m+2)) X² d² f(t)^{m+2}/dt² + (1/6)(m/(m+3)) X³ d³ f(t)^{m+3}/dt³ + … + (1/(M−m)!)(m/M) X^{M−m} d^{M−m} f(t)^M/dt^{M−m}.

Implicit final step (mine): set t = 0. Then f(x)^m = x^m X^{−m}, so [X^{M−m}] f(x)^m = [X^M] x^m. The last displayed term then gives (m/M)[x^{M−m}] f^M = (m/M)[x^{M−m}](x/X)^M, which is the stated result.
errors: No genuine mathematical error found. The apparent sign inconsistency (log vs −log) is a transcription artefact: the manuscript has '−log(1−T/U)' in §1 and §2.

The interchange of the double expansion Σ T^n U^{−n}/n and the collection of the u^{−1} (or u^{−m}) terms is not justified. It is legitimate formally: T^n = O(t^n), and one works in Laurent series in u with power-series coefficients in t. It is also legitimate analytically for |t| < |u| small. Gauss treats it as evident.
In the 'Einfachster Beweis' the specialisation t = 0 and the identification f(x)^m = (x/X)^m are not written out. Without them the final term does not visibly yield the boxed coefficient identity.
Struck-out line (fx^{−m} …) contains coefficient slips; Gauss cancelled it himself.

results.what: Proof of series reversion by comparing the u^{−m} coefficients of −log(1−T/U), expanded once via the factorisation (U−T) = (u−t)·(…) and once as Σ T^n U^{−n}/n. It yields T^m + Σ_{k≥1} (m/(m+k)) [u^k](u/U)^{m+k} T^{m+k} = t^m.
results.modern_name: Lagrange–Bürmann inversion formula, proved by formal residues and a logarithmic two-variable kernel (cf. the Faber/Grunsky generating function log((U−T)/(u−t)))
results.usually_credited_to: Formula: Lagrange (1770), Bürmann (1799). Residue-type proofs: Cauchy (1826), Jacobi (1830, Crelle 6). Log-kernel generating function: Faber (1903), Grunsky (1939) in function theory.

results.what: Reciprocity form for mutually inverse series: [X^M]x^m/m = [x^{−m}]X^{−M}/M = [x^{M−m}](x/X)^M/M.
results.modern_name: Lagrange inversion in coefficient/residue form (Jacobi–Schur reciprocity form)

results.what: Derivation from Lagrange's series for x = t + X f(x) with φ = f^m, using φ′f^n = (m/(m+n))(f^{m+n})′.

deep.surprise_reason: The theorem is classical (Lagrange, Bürmann). The second proof is textbook Lagrange expansion. The first proof is elegant and non-standard for 1813: it is essentially a formal-residue argument using the logarithmic kernel log((U−T)/(u−t)) and coefficient extraction in u^{−m}. That anticipates the spirit of Jacobi's 1830 residue proof and the later Faber/Grunsky generating-function technique. Still, it is a new proof of a known result, and I am unsure whether it appears in Gauss's Werke (vol. X?). Hence notable but modest.

transcription_corrections: §1: the manuscript reads 'Man entwickle −log(1−T/U)'. The minus sign before log is present in the image and dropped in the transcription.
§2: 'also −log(1−T/U) = t/u + tt/2uu + t³/3u³ + etc − log(1+ …)'. The leading minus is present (written 'also−log'). The blot before the second log is a minus sign.
'Ist Sind die Gleichungen': 'Ist' is struck through.
'φx = (fx)^{+m}': the '+' appears written over a former '−', consistent with the struck line beginning 'fx^{−m}'.
Last lines: first term reads 'ft^{+m}'. The final term has factorial 1.2.3…(M−m), with X^{M−m} and d^{M−m}ft^M/dt^{M−m}.
Struck line: the transcription's 'XX ft^{−m}' in the second term is probably 'mX·…' (single X); irrelevant since cancelled.
